newsitem.title: UK: Shortage fears seen pushing LIFFE cocoa higher.
newsitem.headline: Shortage fears seen pushing LIFFE cocoa higher.

text.p: Shortage fears could push LIFFE cocoa prices sharply higher in the near-term, with July climbing to between 1,000 and 1,050 stg per tonne within the next six weeks, several traders said this week.
But analysts, sensing a reprise of last summer's cocoa surge to eight-year highs on shortage fears, only to drop sharply when supply came in higher than expected, remained sceptical.

On Tuesday, traders noted an inversion in the market's structure pointing to a cocoa shortage. July traded near a 16-stg premium to December compared to a 12-stg discount last week, they said. At midday on Wednesday, July was at a 17-stg premium.
"The movement of the structure about 20 stg since last week is telling us there's a problem, that there's not enough cocoa," a trader said.
CSCE July ended on Tuesday at a 43-stg discount to December.

Some traders also noted that European gradings were indicating the market can deliver about 7,600 lots, but open interest in May and July continued to stand high at 36,186 contracts as of Monday's close. Open interest was almost evenly split with July garnering 18,038 lots and May tallying 18,148.
"If physicals stay here (at current levels), then the market has a problem," another trader said.
But analysts sceptical of supply woes said May and July open interest had time to drop with more than a month to delivery.
Lawrence Eagles, analyst with GNI Ltd, said short supply was "possible, but certainly as far as the supply and demand picture goes, there doesn't appear to be any great shortage this year."
Nevertheless, supply fears have helped keep nearby months firm, with July expected to benefit most.
On April 2, May hit 1,050, its highest level in about 7-1/2 months, before fund sales on April 7 drove prices down more than five percent. Cocoa has since been steadily recovering.
If supply worries continue, a trader said July will gain most as short-holders decide whether to deliver, cover or roll forward short positions. He said all options would buoy July.
Though an analyst here also believed supply fears were premature, he said front months could hold a premium for a few months as long as the market believes a shortage is possible.
Traders said supply speculation has been fuelled by expectations that much of the Ivorian mid-crop beans would be too small or defective to reach terminal.

But Eagles noted the Ivorian mid-crop could be poorer than usual but if the crop size is large, the amount of low quality beans could have little market impact because what is accepted could be sufficient to fill the market's needs. If supply suffices, he said July would be more fairly priced near 960.

Instead, Eagles said that what a large trade house which is believed to be holding a big volume of cocoa will do, will be more critical. The trade house could swing prices either way by deciding to buy another pile of cocoa or unleashing some of its holdings.
"It's an extremely volatile situation," he said.
